analysis.investment_thesis: Apollo Micro Systems is a capital-hungry defense electronics assembler growing at 18% revenue CAGR but destroying cash at an accelerating rate (-₹82 Cr FCF in FY25 vs ₹56 Cr net profit), while trading at a preposterous 113x PE and 58x EV/EBITDA for a business earning only 10% ROE. You are paying a compounding-machine price for a working-capital trap.
key_strengths: India defense indigenization tailwind (Atmanirbhar Bharat) creates multi-year order visibility for domestic electronics suppliers
Revenue CAGR 18% and net profit CAGR 32% over 5 years — accelerating in FY25 (₹562 Cr revenue, ₹56 Cr PAT)
Moderate leverage at Debt/Equity 0.33 with healthy promoter holding of 52% providing governance anchor
key_risks: Free cash flow is catastrophically negative (-₹82 Cr in FY25, -₹131 Cr in FY24) against ₹56 Cr reported profit — FCF/Net Income is deeply negative, signaling a working capital or earnings quality crisis
ROIC and ROE (10%) are well below the 15% minimum Munger demands; ROCE of 14% barely clears the bar yet the stock commands a 113x PE
Finance costs grew at 17.8% CAGR to ₹34 Cr — nearly 61% of net profit — and borrowings tripled from ₹117 Cr to ₹361 Cr, meaning growth is debt-funded, not self-financing
red_flags: FCF negative in 4 of last 5 years (-₹16, -₹50, -₹131, -₹82 Cr) — a compounding machine should generate cash, not consume it
Earnings quality test fails badly: reported ₹56 Cr PAT in FY25 but only ₹10 Cr OCF — profits exist only on paper while cash bleeds out
Balance sheet nearly doubled in one year (₹956 → ₹1,782 Cr total assets) suggesting a large equity raise masking operating weakness
113x PE for a 10% ROE assembler of defense electronics — paying a luxury price for a commodity-adjacent business
CWIP tripled to ₹107 Cr in FY25 with ongoing heavy capex (-₹92 Cr) — capital intensity is structurally rising, not declining
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Inversion first: what would make this a terrible investment? A capital-intensive assembler (not designer) of defense electronics with sub-threshold returns, serial cash destruction, and a triple-digit PE multiple. Apollo checks every box. The company earned ₹56 Cr in reported profit in FY25 but generated only ₹10 Cr of operating cash flow, implying a massive working capital build — entirely typical of Indian defense subcontractors who must pre-finance long government payment cycles. The trend is worsening: OCF was -₹76 Cr in FY24 and -₹16 Cr in FY23. This is not a momentary blip; it is structural. A business that cannot convert profits to cash is not compounding wealth — it is manufacturing accounting earnings while consuming real capital through debt and equity issuance.

The valuation is the final insult. At 113x trailing PE, the market is pricing Apollo as if it were a high-ROIC compounder with durable pricing power. The actual ROCE of 14% and ROE of 10% are below what I require even for a mediocre business. Operating margins of 17.6% are decent but not exceptional, and the gross margin of 31% tells you this is an assembler with limited IP leverage. The defense sector tailwind is real — India's ₹6 lakh crore defense budget is a genuine opportunity — but the prize will likely accrue to companies with proprietary technology and strong cash generation, not working-capital-intensive assemblers trading at 58x EV/EBITDA. I would need to see ROIC above 18%, sustained positive FCF, and a PE below 30x before I would even begin a deeper look.
